processing: Ripe pu-erh: sun-dried Yunnan large-leaf tea is piled, moistened and fermented (wo dui), then pressed into a thick brick. One merchant describes the recipe as a simple blend of grades 1 to 9.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking. Like other factory ripe bricks, it is a blend of stored material rather than a seasonal harvest.
appearance_dry: A thick, dense, dark brown brick of mixed-grade leaf, as is usual for old factory ripe bricks.
appearance_liquor: Deep red-brown to near black, clear in a well-stored example.
appearance_wet: Dark brown, soft mixed leaf with broken pieces, as is usual for a ripe brick of mixed grades.
taste_profile: Tasting notes for this brick are scarce; expect what is typical of aged factory ripe pu-erh: earthy, woody and smooth, with the piling character faded by age.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for an aged ripe brick: flake it gently, rinse once or twice, then use water close to boiling.

vintage_note: Sold as an aged collectible by decade or year rather than as a fresh seasonal tea. A 1970s lot has gone through auction at Sotheby's, and a 1990 CNNP 73 brick has been sold by a specialist retailer. Treat any very old date with caution and ask for storage history, since age claims on such bricks are hard to check.
description:
The 73 Thick Brick is a piece of ripe pu-erh history: a dense brick tied to the Kunming Tea Factory and to the very first years of modern piled fermentation in Yunnan. It matters more as a reference point than as an everyday tea.

It is a ripe tea, so the leaf went through wet piling before pressing. One merchant describes the blend as simple, using grades 1 to 9, which would suit a brick made for volume more than for prestige.

Reliable tasting notes are hard to come by. As with other aged factory ripe bricks, you can expect earth and wood with a smooth body, and an old piece should have lost its piling funk. Brew it hot and rinse it first.

On the market it appears mainly as aged stock, sold by decade or year, often at collector prices. Ask where it was stored and be wary of a confident date with nothing behind it.
history:
A Yunnan delegation that included Kunming and Menghai factory staff, along with technicians from Xiaguan, went to Guangdong to study piled fermentation. Back home, Xiaguan worked out the early ripening method and Kunming added further moisture and heat, and the Kunming factory's mass-produced result was the 73 Thick Brick. Retailers call it a prototype of ripe pu-erh and CNNP's first ripe tea, a claim that comes from the trade.

A natural-stored brick described as 1970s went to auction at Sotheby's in 2021. Where the 73 in the name comes from is not firmly documented, although it is often read as a year.
